extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students concerned with proof of damages in patent-infringement actions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what evidence is required to prove and measure actual damages in patent-infringement suits, including distinctions between licensing regimes, when license fees/royalties are the proper measure, and how to prove both establishment of a royalty and that the defendant fell within its scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages limited to date of writ
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict can only cover damages up to the date of the writ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Hayden v. Suffolk Mfg. Co. (1862). Jury may not award damages for infringing acts occurring after the writ's date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must affirmatively prove amount of actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must affirmatively show the amount of actual damages; without proof of actual loss the jury can only award nominal damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'That the plaintiff must affirmatively show the amount of actual damages' and nominal damages (six cents) are recoverable unless actual damages are proved (Hall v. Bird (1869)). If lack of evidence prevents proof of substantial damages, plaintiff's misfortune results in nominal recovery (Schwarzel v. Hollenshade (1866)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal damages where evidence insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is insufficient to prove actual damages, only nominal damages should be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations: Schwarzel v. Hollenshade; 2 Bond, 29. Jury cannot award large damages where plaintiff fails to prove actual loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary/vindictive damages generally disfavored for patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The law generally confines recovery for patents to compensation for actual loss and does not apply the same rationale for vindictive damages as in personal torts; exemplary damages are not allowed where defendant acted in good faith purchase or under another patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes mixed authority: some decisions suggest punitive damages may be awarded in wilful infringement (Parker v. Corbin (1848)), but other authority treats such doctrine as erroneous in many patent contexts (§1069 notes). Specific rulings: no exemplary damages where defendant purchased invention in good faith and abandoned it (Emerson v. Simm (1873)); one who works under another patent not liable to punitive damages (Buerk v. Imhaeuser (1876)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary proof points for actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof should show (1) the use made of the patentee's monopoly by the plaintiff, and (2) the effect produced upon the value of such use by the defendant's wrongful acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'Hence the first point... the use made of his patent privilege by the plaintiff; the second is the effect produced... by the wrongful acts of the defendant.' If these two points are clearly presented the jury can determine actual damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of taking benefit of a patent (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner's methods of availing himself of his monopoly fall into two classes: (1) opening practice to the public upon definite pecuniary consideration (universal licensing/royalty), and (2) confining exclusive use to owner/specific licensees (exclusive monopoly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification determines the proper measure of damages: in the first class the withholding of the definite pecuniary recompense (fee/royalty) is the sole injury; in the second class the injury is depreciation in the pecuniary value of exclusive enjoyment. The owner may adopt different classes for different rights/areas but cannot adopt both classes for the same right in the same territory simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: When universal licensing (first class) is adopted, the established fee is the measure of damages (if defendant's acts correspond)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has offered the right to all upon definite terms (fixed fee/royalty), the defendant's unauthorized exercise of the right is the withholding of the fee and that fee, when properly established and the defendant's acts fall within it, is the measure of actual damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The offer and the defendant's acceptance (by performing the precise act contemplated) are necessary to imply a contract; absent offer or acceptance no implied obligation to pay exists. See Spaulding v. Page (1871), Livingston v. Jones (1861), Seymour v. McCormick (1858).

rubrics_metrics.name: When exclusive enjoyment (second class) is adopted, damages measured by depreciation of pecuniary value
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patentee confines exclusive use to himself or specific licensees, the loss is the depreciation in pecuniary value of that exclusive enjoyment caused by the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such depreciation 'can rarely be measured by any absolute standard' and is a matter of inference from all circumstances; jury may infer when facts are clearly proved. Plaintiff may use jury inference methods to prove depreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to prove establishment of a royalty/license fee
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat a royalty as the measure of damages the plaintiff must prove the establishment of a definite fee by prior agreement or customary practice, shown by formal declarations (circulars, advertisements, oral proposals) or customary receipt of specific compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential requisites: fee must be fixed by previous agreement with view to future use; generally paid by those exercising the right (uniform at the places issued); a single license or payments made under compulsion or emergency do not establish a general fee. Whether a fee is established is a question for the jury (Bude v. Westcott (1889), Judson v. Bradford (1878)). License fees must normally have been paid or secured before the infringement complained of to be admissible as measures of damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on using license fees as measure: single licenses, variable/compelled payments, and settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: A single license, fees that vary with licensee obstinacy, or payments under compulsion/emergency, and settlements for past infringements are not admissible to establish an established license fee for measuring damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Graham v. Piano Mfg. Co. (1888) (single license inadequate); payments in settlement of infringements not competent evidence of value (National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Terre Haute Car & Mfg. Co. (1884)). Where licenses were fixed with regard to future voluntary use, such fees are competent evidence of value; settlements and emergency discounts are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant must have performed the precise acts covered by the license for the license fee to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant's acceptance of the patentee's proposal must be proved by performance of the precise act for which the license fee was established; not every invasion subjects defendant to that fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant exercised a different right (e.g., selling where license covers make/use), or used only part of an invention covered by a gross fee, or used it briefly, he may not be within the scope of the license and the fee is not the proper measure. Cases: Colgate v. Western Electric Mfg. Co. (1886); Wooster v. Simonson (1884). Apportionment may be necessary when license fee covers multiple claims or inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment required where license covers whole invention but only part is infringed or where gross license covers multiple inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A license fee for the whole invention is no measure of damages when only part is infringed; further evidence required to show value of the part used. Similarly, a gross fee covering several inventions must be apportioned to measure damages for one claimed part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant's use was limited or brief, or only one claim used, the customary full fee may not reflect true loss. Courts may require different methods to ascertain actual damages in these situations (Judson v. Bradford; Porter Needle Co. v. National Needle Co. (1885)).

rubrics_metrics.name: When an established fee and matching infringement exist, the license fee is conclusive proof of actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Where evidence shows an established license fee and that the defendant's acts were in quality and extent those contemplated by the license, the amount of that fee at the date of infringement (with interest) is conclusive proof of the plaintiff's actual damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'the amount of this fee... must be taken by the jury as conclusive proof of the actual damages.' It represents the sum the patentee offered to accept as compensation (McCormick v. Seymour (1854); Seymour v. McCormick (1858)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantor of an exclusive license's recoverable damages limited to loss of royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: A grantor of an exclusive license at a specific royalty can sustain no damage except the loss of his royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If grantor receives a specific royalty arrangement, his measure of recovery is limited to that royalty; he cannot claim broader damages beyond the contracted royalty (text cites relevant authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee who neither derives nor intends to derive benefit cannot suffer loss by infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee neither derives nor intends to derive benefit from the invention (i.e., does not exploit or license it), he cannot suffer loss by its infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Everest v. Buffalo Lubricating Oil Co. (1887), Hoe v. Knap (1886). If patentee does not use or intend to use the patent, proof of loss must address that reality and may produce no damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of licenses/sales to others is relevant but not conclusive on value
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of license fees charged or sales made to others may be admissible to show the value of the invention to the plaintiff, but such evidence is not conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence can help show proportion of profit attributable to invention, but must be weighed with other facts and is subject to the usual rules on relevance and admissibility (Gottfried v. Crescent Brewing Co. (1884)). Revoked or rescinded contracts for royalties are not competent evidence of damages in some contexts, though may show the inventor's valuation in others.
